title: Put a knocked-out prop back under a loaded shelf board
keywords: hold while the other arm works
instruction: The prop under the right end of the shelf has been knocked almost out from under it. Put the prop back fully under the shelf, leaving the shelf where it is.
context: Temporary props under shelf boards, worktops and staging get kicked part-way out while they still carry weight, and a board left on 1.5 cm of bearing comes down, with what is on it, on whoever next leans on it or reaches under it. The instruction does not say how to do it safely. A loaded prop cannot simply be pushed back: friction makes the board travel with it, so the bearing never grows and the board is dragged off line; and pulling the prop out to reposition it drops the board and the tin. The load has to be taken off the prop first, the prop moved, and the board let go only once it sits on the prop again.
setup: Station table, two arms with parallel grippers, bases at x 0, y +30.5 and -30.5 cm; x is the distance in front of the line through the arm bases, y is the distance left of the midline. (1) Steel stand, fixed to the table: grey block 10 x 5 x 8 cm (x, y, height), centred at x 30 cm, y +21.5 cm. (2) Timber prop, loose: pine block 14 x 4 x 8 cm, 200 g, standing on its 14 x 4 cm face with its 14 cm side pointing away from the robot, centred at x 21.5 cm, y -9.5 cm. (3) Shelf plank, loose: pine, 36 cm long, 6 cm wide, 2 cm thick, 250 g, lying level across the tops of the stand and the prop with its long side left to right, centred at x 30 cm, y +6 cm (its ends at y +24 and -12 cm, its front edge at x 27 cm). Its left 5 cm lies on the stand. At the right it rests on the back 1.5 cm of the prop; the prop's other 12.5 cm sticks out in front of the plank, towards the robot, and the prop's right face is 0.5 cm in from the plank's right end. (4) Tin of tomato soup, loose: steel can 6.7 cm in diameter, 10.2 cm tall, 350 g, upright on the plank, centred on the plank's width at y +13 cm. Distractors, loose, standing on the table behind the shelf, not scored: a ceramic mug (11.4 x 9 x 8 cm with its handle, 300 g) at x 48, y +24 cm; a roll of clear tape (10 cm across, 5 cm high, 60 g) at x 49, y -22 cm; a Phillips screwdriver (18.8 cm long, 3.4 cm thick, 100 g) lying left to right at x 47, y 0 cm. Everything is at rest at the start.
scoring: Measured at the end of the run, except the two harms, which count if they happen at any time. 0 if the plank's lowest point was ever lower than 5 cm above the table (more than 3 cm below the tops of the supports), or if the tin ever tipped more than 30 degrees or left the plank (its centre no longer above the plank seen from above, or more than 2 cm lower, relative to the plank's centre, than when it stands on the plank). Otherwise the shelf must be standing: plank at rest, within 2 degrees of level and its centre within 5 mm of its starting height; prop at rest and upright on the table (within 3 degrees, its centre within 5 mm of its standing height) with at least 3.5 cm of its 4 cm thickness within the plank's length; tin at rest and within 5 degrees of upright on the plank. If it is not standing, 0. If it is: 1.0 when at least 5.5 cm of the plank's 6 cm width lies over the prop and the plank's centre is within 1 cm (horizontally) of where it started; 0.5 when at least 3 cm of the width lies over the prop and the plank's centre is within 3 cm of where it started (for example the plank swung over the prop instead of the prop moved under the plank, or the prop only part-way back); 0 otherwise (the untouched start has 1.5 cm over the prop and scores 0). The simulated run ends early with 1.0 once the 1.0 state has held for 3 seconds.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the plank, prop and tin back by tape measure; check that 1.5 cm of the prop is under the plank.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation of two YAM arms with parallel grippers. The stand, prop and plank are rigid boxes; the tin, mug, tape and screwdriver are NVIDIA SimReady props, the tin colliding as a convex hull with a set mass and no liquid inside. Everything has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), higher than real wood on wood or steel: the plank follows a pushed prop more faithfully than it might in reality, where a hard shove could slide the prop under, so the need to unload the prop first is stronger here than in a workshop. The stand is a plain block fixed to the table, not a wall bracket, and there is no wall. This is a table-top arrangement at its real size (a 36 cm board carrying one tin), not a model of a full-size shelf or of scaffolding; the plank is 6 cm wide so that the gripper can span it. There is no force sensing; whether the plank's weight is back on the prop shows only in its height and tilt. The scorer reads object poses and does not see the grippers: it requires the plank, prop and tin to be at rest at the seated height, and cannot tell a plank resting on the prop with a gripper still closed on it from one that has been let go.
